words.definition: an individual living thing capable of carrying out life processes
words.example: A tree is an organism that interacts with both living and non-living parts of its environment.

words.definition: a group of organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring under natural conditions
words.example: The giant panda belongs to a distinct species with a limited geographic range.

words.definition: all individuals of one species living in the same area at the same time
words.example: A population of deer may increase when food is abundant and predation is low.

words.definition: all populations of different species living and interacting in the same area
words.example: A coral reef community contains fish, algae, corals and many other organisms.

words.definition: the physical place where an organism normally lives
words.example: Mangrove forests provide habitat for juvenile fish.

words.definition: the role of a species in an ecosystem, including its resource use and interactions
words.example: Two species with very similar niches may compete strongly for the same resources.

words.definition: a community of organisms interacting with each other and with the abiotic environment
words.example: A pond ecosystem includes water, nutrients, plants, animals and decomposers.

words.definition: a living component or biological interaction that affects organisms
words.example: Predation is a biotic factor that can limit prey populations.

words.definition: a non-living physical or chemical component of the environment
words.example: Temperature is an abiotic factor that influences species distribution.

words.definition: a resource or environmental condition that restricts population growth or distribution
words.example: Low nitrogen availability can be a limiting factor for plant growth.

words.definition: the maximum population size that an environment can support sustainably under given conditions
words.example: A deer population may decline after exceeding the carrying capacity of its habitat.

words.definition: a factor whose effect on a population becomes stronger as population density rises
words.example: Disease transmission often increases as a density-dependent factor in crowded populations.

words.definition: a factor that affects populations regardless of their density
words.example: A severe hurricane can reduce a population as a density-independent factor.

words.definition: an interaction in which organisms seek the same limited resource
words.example: Plants may compete for light when growing close together.

words.definition: an interaction in which one organism captures and consumes another
words.example: Wolf predation can influence the size and behaviour of deer populations.

words.definition: an interaction in which one organism benefits while the host is harmed
words.example: Ticks show parasitism by feeding on the blood of mammals.

words.definition: an interaction between species in which both participants benefit
words.example: Pollinating insects and flowering plants often have a mutualistic relationship.

words.definition: an interaction in which one species benefits while the other is neither significantly helped nor harmed
words.example: Barnacles attached to whales are often used as an example of commensalism.

words.definition: the number of individuals of a species per unit area or volume
words.example: Researchers estimate population density by counting individuals within sample plots.

words.definition: the spatial pattern or geographic range in which organisms occur
words.example: Rainfall can strongly influence the distribution of plant species.

words.definition: an autotrophic organism that converts external energy into organic matter
words.example: Green plants act as producers by converting light energy into chemical energy.

words.definition: an organism that obtains energy by feeding on other organisms or organic matter
words.example: A rabbit is a primary consumer when it feeds on grass.

words.definition: an organism that breaks down dead organic material and releases inorganic nutrients
words.example: Fungi are important decomposers in forest ecosystems.

words.definition: an organism that ingests dead organic matter and fragments it during feeding
words.example: Earthworms act as detritivores by consuming decaying plant material.

words.definition: a feeding position in a food chain or food web
words.example: Herbivores generally occupy the second trophic level.

words.definition: a linear sequence showing how energy and matter pass through feeding relationships
words.example: A simple food chain may run from grass to rabbit to fox.

words.definition: a network of interconnected feeding relationships in a community
words.example: A food web shows that most consumers have more than one food source.

words.definition: the total rate at which producers capture energy and store it as organic matter
words.example: Gross primary productivity is usually high in warm, wet tropical forests.

words.definition: the rate at which producers store biomass after subtracting energy used in respiration
words.example: Net primary productivity represents energy available for growth and consumers.

words.definition: a metabolic process that releases usable energy from organic molecules
words.example: Respiration transfers some stored chemical energy to the environment as heat.

words.definition: the mass of living organic material in a defined area or trophic level
words.example: Tree biomass represents a major carbon store in many forests.

words.definition: the percentage of energy transferred from one trophic level to the next
words.example: Ecological efficiency is limited because organisms lose energy through respiration and waste.

words.definition: the movement of energy between organisms or trophic levels
words.example: Only part of the energy in plants is transferred to herbivores.

words.definition: a diagram showing energy flow or energy available at successive trophic levels
words.japanese: エネルギーピラミッド
words.example: A pyramid of energy always narrows toward higher trophic levels.

words.definition: a diagram showing the amount of living material at each trophic level
words.example: Aquatic ecosystems can sometimes have inverted pyramids of biomass.

words.definition: a diagram showing the number of organisms at each trophic level
words.example: One large tree can support many insects, creating an unusual pyramid of numbers.

words.definition: a measure of energy dispersal and disorder that increases during energy transformations
words.example: Entropy increases as energy is transformed and some becomes unavailable for useful work.

words.definition: electromagnetic energy from the Sun reaching Earth
words.example: Solar radiation provides the main energy input for most ecosystems.

words.definition: the process by which producers use light energy to make organic compounds from inorganic substances
words.example: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose.

words.definition: the rate at which consumers convert absorbed food energy into new biomass
words.example: Fish growth contributes to secondary productivity in an aquatic ecosystem.

words.definition: the movement and storage of carbon among the atmosphere, organisms, oceans and rocks
words.example: Combustion and photosynthesis move carbon between major stores in the carbon cycle.

words.definition: the movement and transformation of nitrogen among the atmosphere, soil, water and organisms
words.example: Bacteria drive several important transformations in the nitrogen cycle.

words.definition: the movement of phosphorus through rocks, soils, water and living organisms
words.example: Unlike nitrogen, the phosphorus cycle has no major atmospheric store.

words.definition: the capture and long-term storage of carbon in biomass, soils, oceans or geological formations
words.example: Forest restoration can increase carbon sequestration in vegetation and soil.

words.definition: a reservoir that absorbs more carbon than it releases over a given period
words.example: A growing forest can function as a carbon sink.

words.definition: a reservoir or process that releases more carbon than it absorbs
words.example: Burning fossil fuels is a major carbon source to the atmosphere.

words.definition: the long-term transformation of buried organic material into fossil carbon stores
words.example: Fossilization can lock carbon away for millions of years.

words.definition: the rapid oxidation of fuel that releases energy and produces gases such as carbon dioxide
words.example: Combustion of coal transfers stored carbon to the atmosphere.

words.definition: the breakdown of dead organic matter by biological and chemical processes
words.example: Decomposition returns nutrients from dead leaves to the soil.

words.definition: the conversion of atmospheric nitrogen gas into biologically usable nitrogen compounds
words.example: Some soil bacteria carry out nitrogen fixation in association with legumes.

words.definition: the bacterial oxidation of ammonium into nitrite and then nitrate
words.example: Nitrification increases the nitrate available for plant uptake.

words.definition: the bacterial conversion of nitrate into gaseous nitrogen compounds that return to the atmosphere
words.example: Waterlogged soils often favour denitrification.

words.definition: the conversion of organic nitrogen in dead matter and waste into ammonium
words.example: Decomposers carry out ammonification as organic material breaks down.

words.definition: the downward removal of dissolved substances through soil by percolating water
words.example: Heavy rainfall can cause nitrate leaching from agricultural soils.

words.definition: the physical or chemical breakdown of rock at or near Earth's surface
words.example: Weathering releases phosphate ions from rock into soil and water.

words.definition: the settling and accumulation of particles or dissolved materials as deposits
words.example: Phosphorus can become locked in sediments at the bottom of lakes.

words.definition: an inorganic form of phosphorus that can be absorbed by plants
words.example: Plant roots take up phosphate from soil solution.

words.definition: a storage of a nutrient within a component of an ecosystem
words.example: Soil organic matter is an important nutrient pool.

words.definition: the rate of movement of a nutrient between stores
words.example: Leaf fall creates a nutrient flux from vegetation to litter.

words.definition: human-caused alteration of a natural cycle or environmental process
words.example: Fertilizer use is an anthropogenic disruption of the nitrogen cycle.

words.definition: a large ecological region characterized by climate, vegetation and associated organisms
words.example: Temperature and precipitation help determine which biome develops in a region.

words.definition: the long-term average pattern of weather conditions in a region
words.example: Climate influences productivity, soils and species distribution.

words.definition: short-term atmospheric conditions at a particular place and time
words.example: A single storm is a weather event rather than evidence of a long-term climate trend.

words.definition: a measure of how hot or cold a body or environment is
words.example: Mean annual temperature helps distinguish tropical from polar biomes.

words.definition: water falling from the atmosphere as rain over a given period
words.example: Low rainfall is a major constraint on desert vegetation.

words.definition: incoming solar radiation received by a surface
words.example: Insolation is generally greater near the equator than near the poles.

words.definition: angular distance north or south of the equator
words.example: Latitude affects solar angle and therefore regional climate.

words.definition: height above sea level
words.example: Temperature usually decreases as altitude increases.

words.definition: a persistent movement of seawater that redistributes heat and nutrients
words.example: Warm ocean currents can raise coastal temperatures.

words.definition: the dominant wind direction occurring most frequently in a region
words.example: Prevailing winds can transport moist air from oceans onto land.

words.definition: a warm, wet biome with high productivity and multilayered evergreen vegetation
words.example: Tropical rainforest supports exceptionally high species diversity.

words.definition: an arid biome with very low precipitation and large daily temperature ranges
words.example: Plants in a hot desert often show adaptations that reduce water loss.

words.definition: a cold treeless biome with a short growing season and often permanently frozen subsoil
words.example: Tundra vegetation is dominated by low-growing plants.

words.definition: a cold northern coniferous forest biome with long winters
words.japanese: タイガ・北方針葉樹林
words.example: Spruce and pine commonly dominate the taiga.

words.definition: a mid-latitude biome dominated by broadleaf trees that lose leaves seasonally
words.example: Temperate deciduous forest occurs where rainfall is sufficient and seasons are distinct.

words.definition: a mid-latitude biome dominated by grasses with moderate rainfall and seasonal temperatures
words.example: Fertile soils have made many temperate grasslands important farming regions.

words.definition: a tropical grassland biome with scattered trees and distinct wet and dry seasons
words.example: Fire and grazing help maintain many savanna ecosystems.

words.definition: a graph showing average monthly temperature and precipitation for a location
words.example: A climatograph can help identify the biome associated with a place.

words.definition: a climate-related condition that restricts organism growth, productivity or distribution
words.example: Low temperature is a major climatic limitation in tundra.

words.definition: the global spatial pattern of major ecological regions
words.example: Biome distribution broadly follows patterns of temperature and precipitation.

units.unit: 2.5 Zonation, succession and change in ecosystems

words.definition: a spatial change in community composition along an environmental gradient
words.japanese: 帯状分布・ゾーネーション
words.example: Rocky shores show zonation as species change with height above sea level.

words.definition: the directional change in community composition and ecosystem structure over time
words.example: After disturbance, succession can gradually replace early colonizers with later communities.

words.definition: community development beginning on a newly exposed surface with little or no soil
words.example: Primary succession can begin on bare rock after a glacier retreats.

words.definition: community redevelopment after disturbance where soil or biological remnants remain
words.example: Secondary succession often follows abandoned farmland or forest fire.

words.definition: an early colonizing species able to establish under harsh or disturbed conditions
words.example: Lichens can act as pioneer species on newly exposed rock.

words.definition: a relatively stable late-successional community under a particular set of environmental conditions
words.example: Traditional succession models describe a climax community at the end of a sere.

words.definition: the complete sequence of communities developing during succession at one site
words.example: A sere may progress from pioneer vegetation to woodland.

words.definition: one recognizable community stage within a succession sequence
words.example: Shrubland can be a seral stage between grassland and forest.

words.definition: a species characterized by rapid reproduction, many offspring and low parental investment
words.example: Many weeds behave as r-strategists in recently disturbed habitats.

words.definition: a species characterized by slower reproduction, fewer offspring and greater investment in survival
words.example: Large mammals often show traits associated with K-strategists.

words.definition: an event that disrupts ecosystem structure, resources or community composition
words.example: Storms, fires and human clearing can all act as disturbances.

words.definition: the ability of an ecosystem to resist change or recover after disturbance
words.example: High biodiversity may contribute to ecological stability under some conditions.

words.definition: the return of ecosystem structure or function after disturbance
words.example: Vegetation recovery can begin soon after grazing pressure is removed.

words.definition: the idea that greater biological diversity can increase ecosystem stability
words.example: The diversity-stability hypothesis predicts that species-rich systems may better maintain function after disturbance.

words.definition: a different persistent ecosystem condition that can exist under similar external conditions
words.example: A shallow lake may persist either as clear water with plants or as a turbid algal state.

words.definition: a large and persistent change from one ecosystem state to another
words.example: Overfishing can contribute to a regime shift in a marine food web.

words.definition: a successional process in which earlier species make conditions more suitable for later species
words.example: Nitrogen-fixing pioneers can facilitate the establishment of later plants.

words.definition: a successional process in which established species suppress or delay later colonists
words.example: Dense early vegetation can inhibit tree seedlings by limiting light.

words.definition: a succession model in which later species can establish despite the presence of earlier species because they tolerate low resource levels
words.example: Shade-tolerant trees may replace pioneers under the tolerance model.

words.definition: a stable community maintained by repeated human activity rather than by natural climatic conditions alone
words.example: Regular grazing can maintain grassland as a plagioclimax instead of allowing woodland to develop.
